title: One in Five Renters Now Can't Make Rent — Even Middle-Class Families Are Getting Squeezed
dek: A new Urban Institute study finds a record share of working-age renters missed or fell short on rent last year, with the pain now spreading well beyond the poorest households.
body: Washington loves to tout stock market highs and GDP figures, but a new report out of the Urban Institute shows what's actually happening at kitchen tables across the country: a record share of working Americans can no longer reliably make rent. Researchers from the Urban Institute found that a growing number of renters in the U.S. are struggling to pay for housing each month, with families across every income bracket — not just the poorest — now falling behind.

The numbers are stark. One in five, or 20.0 percent, of working-age renters reported that they did not pay the full amount of rent or were late with a payment at some point in 2025. That's a significant increase from 2024, when about 14% reported being unable to pay their rent, and researchers say it's the highest share on record since the Urban Institute began tracking the measure. A similar share — slightly more than 20 percent — also said they struggled to pay gas, oil or electricity bills last year.

What should alarm anyone paying attention is that this crisis has stopped being confined to the working poor. One in every five middle-income renters surveyed by the institute said that at some point during 2025, they could not afford to pay the full amount of rent when it was due. Middle-class families who were told for years that they'd done everything right — worked hard, paid their bills, avoided debt — are now one bad month away from missing rent like everyone else.

Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute and co-author of the report, put the stakes plainly: 'We have historically observed that low-income renters experience high rates of housing cost-burdens and, as a result, are particularly vulnerable to having to make choices between meeting their family's basic needs or paying rent. And sometimes that results in eviction or homelessness.' The difference now is that the same choice is creeping up the income ladder.

Researchers pointed to mounting economic pressures and the rising costs of everyday necessities as the drivers behind the deterioration. That's a polite, academic way of describing what working families have known for a while: the cost of simply staying housed has outpaced what a paycheck can cover, even as Washington's political class congratulates itself on economic 'resilience.' For a country that still imports hundreds of thousands of new residents every year on top of a housing stock that hasn't kept pace, it's not exactly a mystery why rents keep climbing out of reach for people who were born here and work here.

In fairness, housing economists broadly attribute the affordability crunch to years of underbuilding, restrictive local zoning, and the lingering aftershocks of pandemic-era inflation and interest-rate hikes rather than any single administration's policy — and the survey data reflects conditions gathered in December 2025, capturing pressures that built up over years, not months. It would be unfair to lay this entirely at the feet of any one president.

Still, the trend line is the story: affordability is getting worse, not better, and it's happening to more Americans, not fewer. If the White House wants to convince skeptical voters that its economic agenda is working before the midterms, a report showing record numbers of renters — including the middle class — falling short on rent isn't the evidence it needs.

title: Justice Department Tells Judge: White House Access Is a Privilege, Not a Right — And the Corporate Press Doesn't Get to Demand One
dek: The Trump administration is fighting to keep CNN, MS NOW and Politico locked out of the White House, telling a federal judge the outlets forfeited their credentials by publishing sensitive material and ignoring basic journalistic standards.
body: For years, the same networks that spent their airtime smearing this administration have treated White House press credentials as an entitlement rather than the privilege it actually is. Now the Justice Department is finally saying so in writing. In a late Tuesday court filing, DOJ lawyers told a federal judge flatly that 'access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,' urging him to reject a bid by CNN, MS NOW and Politico to have their credentials restored.

The three outlets sued the president on Monday after his administration stripped their reporters of the White House 'hard passes' that grant access to the grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against Trump on Monday for violating their constitutional rights after his administration revoked White House press credentials to the outlets' journalists. The case landed before U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, who scheduled an emergency teleconference hearing for Wednesday afternoon.

The White House isn't hiding the ball on why it acted. The Trump administration argued the president's ban complies with the First Amendment because the government has at least two compelling reasons for denying the reporters' access: enforcing minimum standards of professionalism for the press and protecting classified information. As officials put it, the president believes basic journalistic standards require calling, asking for comment, and providing a reasonable opportunity for a response — a bar that shouldn't be controversial for anyone who took journalism ethics seriously before Trump derangement set in.

Attached to the brief were letters spelling out exactly what triggered the bans: reports the White House said threatened national security or spread falsehoods, including stories on depleted munitions, negotiations to end the Iran war, security around the East Wing renovation, and a Politico piece that used unnamed sources to brand the Republican midterm convention in Dallas 'a disaster.' The outlets have until 5 p.m. Friday to contest the decision before it becomes final. DOJ also went further, arguing that a 1977 D.C. Circuit precedent requiring notice and a hearing before credentials are pulled is simply wrong and should be overruled outright — a sign this fight could reshape press-access law for good.

This isn't Trump's first run-in with the White House press corps, and it's worth remembering the last one didn't exactly hold up: the same Judge Kelly once ordered CNN's Jim Acosta's pass restored during Trump's first term, finding his due process rights had been violated. The administration is also still fighting the Associated Press in court over its refusal to call the Gulf of Mexico by its new name. Whether the legal ground has shifted enough this time around remains to be seen when Kelly rules.

To be fair to the other side, press freedom advocates and the White House Correspondents' Association have called the move unconstitutional, and the outlets argue in their filing that the ban brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint in an attempt to coerce more favorable coverage and intimidate other newsrooms into self-censoring. That's a serious charge, and courts have historically been skeptical of government retaliation against disfavored viewpoints — even when the coverage in question has been sloppy, agenda-driven, or flatly unfair to a sitting president.

Whatever a judge ultimately decides, Americans outside the Beltway have long suspected the White House press corps operates as an extension of the Democratic Party's messaging shop rather than a neutral check on power. Whether or not this particular ban survives judicial review, the underlying complaint — that a handful of legacy outlets abused their privileged perch to spread anonymously sourced hit pieces — is one plenty of ordinary Americans have been making for a decade.

title: Democrats and Retired Brass Sound Alarm Over Guard at the Polls — But the Real Threat Is Voter Fraud, Not Voter Security
dek: With the midterms 50 days away, Democratic lawmakers and activist groups are stoking fears that Trump will deploy troops to polling places, even as voting officials say they're simply preparing for a secure, orderly election.
body: Six weeks before Americans go to the polls, the Democratic Party's midterm strategy appears to include one thing above all: manufacturing a scandal before it happens. A growing chorus of Democratic lawmakers, retired military officers and left-leaning advocacy groups is demanding assurances that the Trump administration won't deploy the National Guard near polling places this November, even though no such deployment has been ordered.

It's worth noting plainly that federal law does bar armed troops or federal agents from polling places, and both parties agree on that basic fact. Voting officials across the country say they intend to run the midterms as usual and have been preparing contingency plans in case armed federal personnel do show up, but that hasn't stopped an entire cottage industry of lawsuits, Freedom of Information Act requests and public service campaigns from springing up around a hypothetical.

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration last month over records requests about supposed plans to seize ballots, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan has been pressing military leaders and federal agencies to rule out any troop presence at the polls. When Air Force Gen. Gregory Guillot, who oversees U.S. Northern Command, was asked by Sen. Tammy Duckworth what guardrails exist, he said plainly that he didn't think troops should be anywhere near polling places, and that if given such an order he would look at it very closely, hardly the picture of a general itching to carry out martial law at the ballot box.

A retired group calling itself the Former Judge Advocates Working Group has spent months writing to Congress pointing to Trump's executive order labeling Antifa a domestic terrorist organization as supposed evidence of a hidden plan to invoke the Insurrection Act on Election Day. That is a significant leap from an order aimed at a violent extremist network to a conspiracy theory about troops at your local high school gymnasium polling place.

To their credit, the concerns raised by these critics deserve a fair hearing: no president of either party should use military force to intimidate voters, and it is entirely legitimate for Congress and watchdog groups to demand clarity from the administration on its plans. Voters have every right to know the rules ahead of time, and the administration would be wise to state clearly and often that troops will not be stationed at polling sites.

But there's a difference between healthy vigilance and a coordinated pressure campaign designed to cast doubt on the legitimacy of an election that hasn't even happened yet. For years, Democrats dismissed concerns about noncitizen voting and ballot security as right-wing paranoia; now the same voices are the ones spinning worst-case scenarios about the military. If Democratic officials and legacy media outlets spent half as much energy demanding secure voter rolls and verified citizenship as they do imagining troops at the ballot box, American elections might inspire a lot more public confidence than they currently do.

title: Missouri's GOP Map Heads Back to the Supreme Court as Democrats Try Every Trick to Block the Will of Voters
dek: A federal appeals panel sided with the Trump-backed Missouri congressional map, but map opponents raced to the Supreme Court late Tuesday in a bid to keep a Democrat-friendly district on the books.
body: Missouri Republicans just won another round in the courts, and Democrats are once again running to the Supreme Court to try to stop the voters' representatives from doing their job. A three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that Missouri must use the new GOP-drawn congressional map for the November election rather than reverting to the old lines Democrats prefer.

The panel didn't mince words. It found that flipping maps this late in the cycle after voters already picked their nominees in the August primary would be unconstitutional chaos. As the judges put it, the Constitution does not permit Missouri to use a different congressional district map in the November 2026 general election than it used in the August 2026 primary election.

This is not some partisan hack job from Trump-appointed judges alone. The panel included Judge James Loken, an appointee of George H.W. Bush, alongside two Trump appointees, Judges David Stras and Justin Smith. Even a judge with no connection to this administration looked at the facts and reached the same conclusion Republicans have been making all along.

The new map, which splits the Kansas City-area 5th District, would likely cost Democrats one of their two Missouri-based seats currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, and that's exactly why the left is fighting so hard to stop it. Never mind that Missouri lawmakers passed this map through the ordinary legislative process under a Republican governor and Republican legislature responding to President Trump's call to protect the GOP's razor-thin House majority.

Predictably, opponents of the map filed an emergency appeal at the Supreme Court late Tuesday night, the third time this fight has landed before the justices. The high court has twice before sided against the new map and has given map supporters until midday Wednesday to respond to the latest emergency plea.

To be fair to the other side, critics of the map make a real legal argument: Missouri's own Supreme Court ruled that the new districts cannot take effect unless voters approve them in a referendum, and opponents say they already gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures to force that statewide vote. County election officials also warn that switching maps now, after absentee ballots have already gone out to military and overseas voters, would be a logistical nightmare.

Still, Republicans see this fight as part of a much bigger picture. Democrats in California just rammed through their own aggressive gerrymander to manufacture up to five new seats, yet the same voices demanding Missouri stick with old maps had nothing to say about that power grab. If Democrats get to redraw the map to their advantage in blue states, Missourians should not be forced to play by a different set of rules just because the outcome might help Republicans keep control of Congress.

title: Vance Task Force Purges 760,000 'Phantom' Obamacare Enrollees, Saves Taxpayers $2.2 Billion
dek: Vice President JD Vance says a sweeping anti-fraud crackdown is removing hundreds of thousands of bogus and ineligible Obamacare enrollments, part of a broader effort to root out waste that has drained American taxpayers for years.
body: For years, working Americans have paid the price for a broken Obamacare system that Washington let insurance brokers and fraudsters exploit at will. Now the Trump administration is finally doing something about it. Vice President JD Vance announced Tuesday that his White House Fraud Task Force will strike 750,000 fraudulently enrolled people from the ACA exchanges, a move he said will save U.S. taxpayers $2.2 billion.

Standing alongside Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Vance laid out just how brazen the scheme had become. He described one fraud ring that had 40 agents, 40 brokerage agents who had funneled 50,000 people into the Obamacare system fraudulently, adding that many of those people quite literally didn't even exist.

An additional 419,000 enrollees will face enhanced verification of their legal residency and income before they can keep their subsidies. Vance was blunt about why that matters: we're going to make sure that they are, first of all, legal residents of the United States of America, and second of all, we're going to make sure that they actually meet the income threshold requirements in order to receive these Obamacare benefits.

The administration also announced a six-month moratorium on new brokers signing up enrollees, targeting the middlemen officials say pocketed commissions for stuffing the exchanges with fake or ineligible names. Vance did not hold back on who he blames for letting the racket flourish, faulting the Biden administration for a system that rewarded brokers, that made people rich for enrolling fake people in programs that are meant to ensure that our fellow citizens have health care, calling it a scandal in his own words.

Dr. Oz was even more direct about the scale of the deception, telling reporters these are not real people and that the government is not paying insurance for nonexistent ghosts. Officials pointed to enrollments that lacked valid Social Security numbers or proper immigration documentation as a driving factor behind the fraud, precisely the kind of loophole this administration has pledged to close across every federal program.

Democrats, naturally, are crying foul. Rep. Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, claimed Republicans have already created the worst healthcare crisis ever and accused the administration of making coverage harder to access. Some healthcare policy experts have also raised questions about the transparency of the process and whether legitimate low-income Americans could be swept up alongside genuine fraudsters, a fair concern the administration should be held to as it moves forward.

But the bigger picture is undeniable: an independent Congressional Budget Office analysis last year estimated 2.3 million ACA enrollees improperly claimed premium tax credits, and outside estimates have put total improper subsidies at nearly $25 billion. After years of Washington looking the other way while insurance companies and brokers gamed a system meant for American families, it's about time someone started making sure taxpayer dollars actually go to the people they were meant to help.

title: Beijing Slow-Walks Soybean and Rare Earth Promises Even as Xi Enjoys the Red-Carpet Treatment
dek: Ahead of Thursday's summit, an uneven delivery record on soybeans, Boeing jets and rare earths shows just how little of last year's trade truce China has actually honored.
body: While Xi Jinping is feted with a state dinner and a military honor guard in Washington this week, the fine print of last year's U.S.-China trade truce tells a far less flattering story about Beijing's follow-through. According to CNBC, the headline commitments underpinning the truce — soybean purchases, Boeing aircraft orders and access to rare earth elements — are progressing at markedly different speeds ahead of Thursday's summit between Trump and Xi, with analysts saying the uneven record shows Beijing has little intention of ceding real strategic leverage.

The soybean numbers are the clearest evidence of the gap between promise and delivery. China, still the world's largest soybean importer, saw the American share of its soybean imports plummet from 40% before Trump's 2018 tariffs to just 23% in the first five months of 2026 — this despite White House claims that Beijing committed at the Busan Summit to buy 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans annually through 2028, on top of another $17 billion a year in agricultural purchases pledged during Trump's May visit to China.

The Boeing side of the ledger is murkier still. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that roughly 140 aircraft out of a promised 200-jet commitment are in a "good state," with orders for another 10 being written — but customers, aircraft models and delivery timelines remain undisclosed. Boeing's own CEO, Kelly Ortberg, has downplayed expectations of any single splashy 200-jet announcement, saying individual Chinese airlines will place and reveal orders on their own timeline, which conveniently keeps Beijing's leverage intact for as long as it wants.

One analyst put it bluntly to CNBC: "The truce is moving fastest where it costs least," said Eric Xiao, head of sales for Asia at CMC Markets — a polite way of saying Beijing is happy to buy soybeans it needs anyway while continuing to sit on the rare earth supply chain American manufacturers and defense contractors actually depend on.

That rare earth leverage is the real story here, and it is the one American voters should care about most. Beijing controls the global supply chain for materials like yttrium, scandium, neodymium and indium — the building blocks of everything from smartphones to fighter jets — and every year Washington fails to build a domestic mining and refining base is another year American manufacturing and national security remain hostage to the goodwill of a Communist government that has shown, purchase order by purchase order, exactly how much its promises are worth.

Farm groups and some in the business community counter that even partial, imperfect progress is better than the outright trade war that preceded it, and that soybean farmers and aircraft workers benefit from any increase in Chinese orders regardless of whether Beijing hits every target on paper. Economists in that camp warn that pushing Beijing too hard right before the midterms risks reigniting a tariff war that would hit American consumers just as inflation numbers are already souring voters on the president's economic stewardship.

But goodwill is not a strategy, and neither is a state dinner. If this week's summit produces nothing more than another vague joint statement while rare earth shipments and soybean purchases continue to lag behind the promises made in Busan and Beijing, American workers and farmers will have paid the price for pageantry rather than policy.

title: Trump Rolls Out the Red Carpet for Xi as Communist China's Leader Lands in Washington
dek: President Trump personally greeted Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusual honor for the leader of America's chief strategic rival as a three-day state visit gets underway.
body: Chinese leader Xi Jinping touched down at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday to a greeting American presidents rarely extend to foreign heads of state: Donald Trump himself, waiting on the tarmac. According to the Associated Press, Trump's decision to greet Xi at the airport just outside Washington rather than waiting for him at the White House shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China's leader as he makes his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade.

The full itinerary, released by the Office of the First Lady, is heavy on pageantry. On Thursday, Trump and Melania Trump will host a State Arrival Ceremony on the South Lawn featuring 479 military personnel representing every branch of the armed forces, followed by a Rose Garden guard-of-honor review before the two leaders sit down for their summit. That evening brings a formal State Dinner in the East Room. Friday morning, the Xi and Peng Liyuan will be received again for tea in the White House Red Room before departing.

The visit marks Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan's first trip back to the White House in more than a decade, and it comes just four months after Trump made his own state visit to Beijing in May. The two leaders first met in Trump's second term at last October's Busan Summit, where Trump invited Xi to Washington "at an appropriate time."

Asked why her husband would break with protocol to personally welcome the head of the Chinese Communist Party at a military base rather than the executive residence, First Lady Melania Trump said simply that Trump decided to do it because "they have a great relationship." That may be true between the two men. It is less clear that the relationship has been great for American workers, who have watched Beijing slow-walk soybean purchases and rare-earth commitments even as it collects the diplomatic trophy of a full state visit — flyovers, honor guards and a White House state dinner included.

For a regime that has spent decades gutting American manufacturing, stealing intellectual property and building up its military with the proceeds of a lopsided trade relationship, the full honors of a state visit are a remarkable gift. Past administrations of both parties have made the mistake of assuming that pageantry and personal rapport with China's leader translate into real concessions. Voters who backed Trump on the promise of putting America first will be watching Thursday's summit to see whether this visit produces enforceable commitments on trade and rare-earth supply chains, or merely more photo opportunities for Beijing's propaganda apparatus.

Supporters of the outreach argue that state visits are standard diplomatic tools and that keeping channels open with Beijing lowers the risk of a wider conflict at a moment when the U.S. is already tied down by the war in Iran. Business groups and farm-state lawmakers note that any thaw, even an uneven one, has already helped move Chinese purchases of American soybeans and aircraft, and they credit the summit format with keeping trade talks from collapsing into open confrontation.

Whether this week's ceremony produces anything beyond handshakes and toasts will be clear soon enough. Thursday's summit meeting is where the substance — on tariffs, rare earths, and the fentanyl trade Beijing has long been accused of enabling — will actually be negotiated, away from the cameras.

title: Poll: Trump Sinks to New Lows on the Economy as Six-Week Countdown to Midterms Begins
dek: A new CNN survey finds just 27% of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of the economy, a warning sign for Republicans as voters put affordability at the top of their list.
body: Republicans are staring down a rougher midterm landscape than the one that cost them the House in 2018, according to a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS. With President Trump at record unpopularity, voters say they prefer Democratic congressional candidates over Republicans by an eight-point margin — slightly smaller than the 12-point Democratic advantage CNN found at this point in 2018, but Trump himself is polling even worse than he did that year, and the economic mood has soured considerably since then.

The numbers on the economy are the starkest sign of trouble. Just 27% of Americans now approve of Trump's handling of the economy, down 22 points from where he stood in 2018, and only 28% describe economic conditions as good, a 41-point collapse. Two-thirds of registered voters now call the economy "extremely important" to their vote, a higher share than heading into either of the last two midterm elections — meaning the issue that once powered Trump's political brand is now the one dragging his numbers down.

A separate NBC News poll released earlier this week found similar erosion. Trump's approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low, with a majority — 55% — saying they believe his policies have hurt the economy, up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed gas prices and the cost of living back into the headlines. Democrats now hold a five-point edge in the generic congressional ballot in that poll, 50% to 45%.

None of this is happening in a vacuum. The war against Iran, now approaching its seventh month, has scrambled fuel markets and short-circuited the White House's ability to tout the parts of the economic record still working in Trump's favor — including Census data showing median household income hit an all-time high last year. The White House has pushed back on the gloomier reading of the numbers, with spokesman Kush Desai telling NBC News that "the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the President's long-term economic agenda on the home front," while acknowledging "temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict."

It is worth asking how much of this polling slump reflects Trump's actual record versus a Beltway press corps and Democratic machine eager to nationalize every gas-pump complaint into a referendum on the president six weeks before an election. Household income is up. Wages have outpaced inflation for much of this year. But there is no denying that voters feel the pinch at the pump and in the grocery aisle, and no amount of spin from either party changes what people pay for gas and groceries — a lesson every incumbent eventually learns the hard way.

Democrats and independent pollsters counter that the numbers reflect genuine kitchen-table pain rather than manufactured outrage, pointing out that Trump's own party is more pessimistic about the economy than at almost any point in his presidency and that Republicans' shrinking but still-real advantage in the generic ballot could evaporate entirely if gas and grocery prices don't ease before November.

With six weeks left before Americans vote, the numbers leave Republicans defending their House and Senate majorities against a headwind that looks less like a normal midterm correction and more like a genuine referendum on the cost of living under this administration.

body: Lonnie G. Bunch III, the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, announced on September 8 that he will retire at the end of 2026. The Board of Regents has launched a national search and has not named a successor.

"It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement," Bunch said. He told NPR that the president's criticism of the Smithsonian wasn't part of his decision, while stressing the institution's independence. "The work we do explains the complexity of America," he said.

The conflict has been building for more than a year. In August 2025, President Trump called for a "comprehensive internal review" of eight Smithsonian museums and directed them to "celebrate American exceptionalism." In July 2026, the administration released a report accusing the National Museum of American History of "extreme political activism."

Bunch has had a historic career. He was the Smithsonian's first historian and first Black secretary, and he founded the National Museum of African American History and Culture. That record deserves respect, and so do the difficult chapters of American history the museums hold.

The populist complaint was never about telling hard truths. It was about tone. Families who paid for these institutions with their taxes walked through exhibits that seemed more interested in indicting the country than explaining how it became the freest and most prosperous nation in history. Complexity and pride can exist side by side.

The next secretary should be judged on whether a kid from Milwaukee or Midland leaves the Mall more proud of being American and better informed about the country's history. Critics warn that political pressure on museums threatens scholarly independence. The Regents' choice will show which view wins.

body: President Trump said Monday that his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with an Iranian delegation for three hours on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, and that the meeting "went very well."

Trump told reporters that another session is planned for the "very near future" and framed the choice facing Tehran in stark terms: "It's potential greatness, or obliteration." He said Iran "wants to talk to us" and that "the relationship is developing."
The president also said he expects to sign an agreement "right after" the November midterm elections. Asked about the talks, Witkoff said he felt "very good right now."

For voters who backed Trump on a promise of strength without endless foreign entanglements, this is the test: pressure first, then a deal that puts American interests ahead of the globalist consensus that shaped past Iran agreements. The details, which the White House has not released, will decide whether that promise holds.

Critics will note that the war with Iran remains one of the issues weighing on voters heading into November, and that a deal timed to land after Election Day spares the administration from having its terms judged at the ballot box.

Also Monday, Trump met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, where he said he was unfamiliar with the UK's decision to sanction Israeli settlements, although officials had reportedly briefed him on it beforehand.

body: Customs and Border Protection says it has now gone 16 straight months without releasing a single migrant into the country at the southern border, the kind of number that was unthinkable during the surge years.

Apprehensions fell 5 percent from July to August, according to a monthly roundup of federal data. Of those caught, 88 percent were single adults and 64 percent were Mexican citizens. Rio Grande Valley in South Texas remained the busiest sector.

Enforcement capacity is growing. Border Patrol has more than 2,200 trainees in its academy, the largest cadre in its history, and plans a new 87-acre station near Tucson. The U.S. military has shot down about 300 suspected cartel drones this year, and cartel drone activity reportedly fell 75 percent after laser systems were deployed alongside 800 Mexican troops.

Wall construction is facing resistance. On September 14 a coalition of 230 landowners in the Big Bend region filed the sixth lawsuit challenging the federal waivers used to speed up construction, citing ranches, river access and family graves. In Arizona's San Rafael Valley, three protesters were arrested September 15 at a construction site.

The administration's supporters see the numbers as proof that the border was always a question of will, not resources. Opponents point to other costs in the same reporting: overcrowded detention sites, deportations to third countries such as Equatorial Guinea, and an ICE whistleblower alleging lowered hiring standards.
The legal fights in Texas are the ones to watch. Private property rights matter to conservatives too, and how the government handles the Big Bend landowners will shape how durable the wall is.

body: The George W. Bush Institute published its September immigration update on Monday. Its conclusion is meant as a warning: current policies will cut legal immigration by 33 to 50 percent by the end of President Trump's second term, meaning 1.5 million to 2.4 million fewer legal immigrants.

The report, by immigration policy director Laura Collins, lists the changes. Refugee admissions totaled 10,258 in the first ten months of fiscal 2026, compared with 38,102 for all of fiscal 2025. Student visa issuance fell 23 percent in 2025, and F-1 visas fell 33.4 percent. Naturalization applications dropped 74 percent this year.
Its figure of the month is $103,265, the proposed fee for most new H-1B applications for skilled foreign workers.

From the populist side, much of this list reads as a scorecard of promises kept. H-1B visas have long been used to replace American tech workers with cheaper labor, and a six-figure fee forces employers to prove they can't hire here first. Lower overall numbers are what the voters who elected this administration asked for.

The report also points to problems that aren't a matter of ideology. USCIS has a record 12.1 million pending cases while processing fewer applications than in any year in over a decade, and the employment-based green card backlog exceeds 1.2 million. A system that lets people wait forever is not an immigration policy. Whatever the number of admissions, the agency should decide cases quickly.
Business groups and the Bush Institute argue the cuts will cost the economy workers and talent. That debate will keep going through November. The immigration restriction side is winning it for now.
dek: A new report projects 1.5 to 2.4 million fewer legal immigrants by the end of Trump's term, and puts the proposed H-1B fee at $103,265.

title: Bush Think Tank Warns Legal Immigration Could Fall by Up to Half. Voters Asked for Exactly That

body: Election Day is November 3, and Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both the House and the Senate. That margin is thin enough that a small drop in base turnout could hand Democrats the gavel.

NPR reports that a Senate map once seen as friendly to Republicans has become competitive, with races in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska in play. In Texas, Republican nominee Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico. The Washington Post reported last week that Democrats feel increasingly confident about taking control of Congress.

Voters' concerns cover the war in Iran, immigration, tariffs, gas prices and the overall cost of living. NPR also reports that the president's approval ratings are at record lows and that voters see a gap between their priorities and the White House's.

For the America First movement, the lesson is not to turn away from the border and trade fights that won in 2024, but to connect them to the kitchen table. Fewer workers competing for jobs, tariffs that bring factories home, and energy that lowers prices at the pump are the argument. Candidates who make it clearly will outrun the polls.

Democrats are betting affordability decides the election and that their voters are more motivated. Polls have favored them on the House. The next six weeks will show whether Republicans can close that gap.
dek: Senate races in Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska have turned competitive, and Democrats are feeling bullish. Turnout among the base will decide it.
